The trial of the 66-year-old man, better known as Duch, resumed Monday just outside the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh. Spectators, many of them survivors of the abuse, watched the proceedings from an auditorium separated from the courtroom by a large glass window. The proceedings began with Duch offering a basic introduction of himself. Court officials then read out the findings of their lengthy investigation. Prosecutors contend Duch ran S-21, a prison that had been converted from a school. Here, men, women and children were shackled to iron beds and tortured -- before they were beaten to death, prosecutors said. Many of the victims were military officials or Communist Party members targeted for not going along with the philosophy of the ultra-Maoist Khmer Rouge movement, prosecutors said. Duch faces charges that include crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture and murder. He has admitted his role in the Khmer Rouge's genocidal reign.  Watch why his trial is significant » . The movement swept to power in 1975. Three years, eight months and 20 days later, at least 1.7 million people -- nearly one-quarter of Cambodia's population -- were dead from execution, disease, starvation and overwork, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. The non-profit organization has been at the forefront of recording the atrocities committed during the Khmer Rouge regime. S-21 was one of 189 similar institutions across Cambodia. Duch is the first former Khmer Rouge leader to stand trial. The tribunal, which is made up of Cambodian and international judges, does not have the power to impose the death penalty. If convicted, Duch faces from five years to life in prison. The trial is expected to last three or four months. "Probably the most important thing about this court is: even after 35 years, you are still not going to get away with it. That is the message," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit. Even though Duch was not a senior leader with the movement, many Cambodians were relieved that one of the regime's former leaders was facing justice, said Youk Chhang, head of the Documentation Center of Cambodia. "I think there is a feeling of, well you know, finally -- now it's finally happening after all these years of waiting -- hearing, fighting, negotiating," he told CNN last month. "People have that kind of sense of relief that it's now moving. When I ask people around the center today, people say, 'Oh, it's about time.'" Four of the regime's former leaders, also accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, await trial before the tribunal. The regime's leader, Pol Pot, died in 1998. "It all seems so fresh," said Norng Champhal, who was a starving little boy when Vietnamese forces invaded the prison. He was separated from his mother after a night in the prison and never saw her again. "It's hard to control my feelings when I see this," he said, as he watched footage of the prison taken 30 years ago. "I wonder whether my parents were tortured like these people," he said. CNN's Dan Rivers contributed to this report.

Convened just outside the capital of Phnom Penh, the trial drew numerous spectators—many of them survivors of the regime—who observed the proceedings from an auditorium separated from the courtroom by a large glass partition. 

The session opened with Duch offering a brief self-introduction, after which court officials read the findings of an extensive investigation. Prosecutors asserted that Duch directed S-21, a former secondary school converted into a notorious detention facility. Within its walls, victims were shackled to iron beds, tortured, and ultimately beaten to death. Many of those targeted were military personnel or Communist Party officials accused of ideological deviance from the ultra-Maoist movement.

Duch faces charges of crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture, and murder. He has previously admitted his role in the Khmer Rouge’s genocidal era. 

The proceedings underscore a pivotal moment in history. The Khmer Rouge seized power in 1975. During its rule—lasting three years, eight months, and twenty days—at least 1.7 million people, nearly a quarter of Cambodia's population, perished from execution, disease, starvation, and forced labor, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. "Perhaps the most critical message of this court is that even after 35 years, impunity is not an option," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit.

Although Duch was not a member of the regime's inner circle, many Cambodians expressed profound relief that a key figure was finally being held accountable, noted Youk Chhang, director of the Documentation Center of Cambodia.

The historic trial of former Khmer Rouge prison chief Kaing Guek Eav, widely known as "Duch," has officially resumed before a United Nations-backed tribunal in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. As the first senior figure of the brutal communist regime to face legal judgment, Duch’s proceedings mark a critical and long-awaited moment of legal accountability for a nation still haunted by the legacy of mass atrocities.

At the heart of the prosecution’s case is Duch’s direct command of the notorious Tuol Sleng interrogation center, code-named S-21. **PHNOM PENH** — In a quiet, high-security courtroom on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, history and accountability finally collided. The U.N.-backed Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC) officially resumed the landmark trial of Kaing Guek Eav, the infamous former Khmer Rouge commander widely known as "Duch." Facing a panel of national and international judges, the former mathematics teacher turned prison warden was formally confronted with a mountain of forensic and documentary evidence, charging him with war crimes, torture, and crimes against humanity.

The resumption of the trial marks a critical juncture for the hybrid tribunal, which was established to deliver long-delayed justice for the atrocities committed during the ultranationalist communist regime's reign from 1975 to 1979. 

At the center of the prosecution’s case is S-21, or Tuol Sleng, a former Phnom Penh high school that Duch transformed into a terrifyingly efficient center for interrogation, torture, and extermination. Prosecutors painstakingly detailed how Duch was not merely a passive bureaucrat following orders, but an active, meticulous architect of human suffering. Utilizing thousands of recovered prison logs, forced confessions, and photographic archives, the prosecution demonstrated that Duch personally overseen the brutal interrogation techniques—including waterboarding, electric shocks, beating, and medical experimentation—inflicted on men, women, and children deemed "traitors" to the revolution.

The evidence presented revealed an unyielding bureaucracy of murder. Duch kept precise records, signing off on execution lists with cold administrative notes such as "kill them all" or "destroy." Of the estimated 15,000 to 20,000 prisoners who entered S-21’s barbed-wire gates, only a handful survived. Most were stripped of their humanity, tortured until they signed absurd, fabricated confessions of foreign espionage, and then driven to the nearby Choeung Ek killing fields to be executed.

While Duch has uniquely acknowledged his guilt and expressed remorse—a stark contrast to other surviving high-ranking Khmer Rouge officials who have maintained innocence or ignorance—his defense team has sought to mitigate his liability by portraying him as a middle-level functionary operating under constant fear for his own life. However, the tribunal’s detailed investigative findings paint a far more damning portrait of a man who passionately refined the regime’s terror apparatus.

The proceedings carry immense weight for Cambodia, a nation still haunted by the scars of a revolution that wiped out an estimated 1.7 million people—nearly a quarter of the country's total population at the time. Under the radical vision of Pol Pot, the Khmer Rouge attempted to reset society to "Year Zero," forcibly evacuating cities, abolishing currency, religion, and family ties, and subjecting the population to forced labor, starvation, and mass purges.

For the survivors, many of whom traveled from rural provinces to sit in the courtroom gallery or testify as civil parties, the trial represents an overdue validation of their suffering. As the tribunal moves forward, Duch’s trial stands as a monumental step toward ending decades of impunity. Beyond establishing the legal guilt of one man, the proceedings serve as an indispensable historical record, offering a grieving nation a measure of truth, closure, and legal reckoning for the millions of lives lost to the darkness of the Khmer Rouge regime.

**Shadows of the Past: Remembering Tuol Sleng**

In the heart of Phnom Penh, Cambodia, stands a site that embodies one of the darkest and most tragic chapters in modern human history. Known today as the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, this quiet compound of buildings was once Tuol Svay Prey High School. However, between 1975 and 1979, under the brutal communist regime of the Khmer Rouge led by Pol Pot, the former place of learning was transformed into a site of unimaginable horror: Security Prison 21 (S-21), commonly referred to simply as Tuol Sleng.

During the Khmer Rouge’s four-year reign, Tuol Sleng served as the central interrogation and detention facility for suspected enemies of the revolution. The transformation was swift and terrifying. Classrooms were partitioned into cramped, suffocating brick and wooden cells. Playgrounds were altered to hold instruments of torture, and windows were encased in barbed wire to prevent prisoners from taking their own lives. 

An estimated 18,000 to 20,000 men, women, and children were imprisoned at Tuol Sleng. The regime maintained a meticulous bureaucracy of death, taking stark black-and-white photographs of almost every inmate upon arrival. These haunting portraits capture expressions of fear, confusion, defiance, and despair. Prisoners were subjected to horrific physical and psychological torture to force false confessions of treason. Once a confession was signed or recorded, the victims were bound, driven to the nearby Choeung Ek "Killing Fields," and executed. Out of the thousands brought through the gates of S-21, fewer than a dozen survived.

When Vietnamese forces liberated Phnom Penh in January 1979, the horrific truth of Tuol Sleng was revealed to the world. Shortly after, the Cambodian government preserved the facility as a museum to honor the victims, document the genocide, and educate future generations.

Today, visiting Tuol Sleng is a deeply somber experience. The museum remains largely as it was found in 1979. Rusted iron bedframes sit in empty rooms, and thousands of victim photographs hang on display, staring out at visitors from across the decades. The quiet breeze blowing through the frangipani trees in the courtyard offers a stark, poignant contrast to the atrocities committed within the concrete walls.

Tuol Sleng stands as a vital, painful pillar of Cambodia’s national memory. For the people of Cambodia, it is a place of mourning, but also a monument to human resilience and the enduring quest for justice. For the rest of the world, it serves as an uncompromising reminder of the devastating consequences of extremism, hatred, and total silence in the face of tyranny.

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (CNN)** — A landmark UN-backed tribunal in Cambodia has sentenced Kaing Guek Eav, the notorious Khmer Rouge prison commander better known as "Duch," marking the first conviction of a senior official from the murderous regime that devastated the Southeast Asian nation in the late 1970s.

The 67-year-old former math teacher was found guilty of crimes against humanity, war crimes, murder, and torture for overseeing Tuol Sleng—the former high school converted into the infamous S-21 interrogation center where thousands of men, women, and children were systematically tortured before being sent to their deaths.

Duch sat motionless in the courtroom, staring straight ahead as the judge read the historic verdict, concluding a months-long trial that offered a harrowing look into one of the 20th century’s worst atrocities. 

### 'The bureaucrat of death'

Under Duch’s meticulous leadership between 1975 and 1979, S-21 operated as the administrative heart of the Khmer Rouge’s security apparatus. An estimated 15,000 to 18,000 people entered the prison during his tenure. Fewer than a dozen survived.

Unlike other top Khmer Rouge figures who denied knowledge of the atrocities, Duch acknowledged his role as the chief administrator of the prison. During the trial, prosecutors presented a trove of chilling evidence, including detailed execution logs, written torture orders, and photos of victims taken by guards under Duch’s strict supervision.

"He was the bureaucrat of death," said trial observer and human rights advocate Helen Jarvis. "He didn't just follow orders; he refined the system of torture and execution with terrifying efficiency."

Prisoners at S-21 were subjected to waterboarding, electrocution, and severe beatings to force false confessions of treason before being transported to the "Killing Fields" of Choeung Ek, a orchard outside Phnom Penh, where they were executed and buried in mass graves.

### Victims voice mixed emotions

For the few remaining survivors who watched the proceedings from the packed public gallery, the verdict brought a wave of intense emotion. 

"I have waited more than 30 years for this day," said Chum Mey, 79, one of the handful of men who survived S-21 because of his skills in repairing machinery. "Nothing can bring my family back—my wife and child were killed—but today, there is finally some justice."

However, the sentence sparked mixed reactions outside the courtroom. The judges originally handed down a 35-year sentence, which was reduced due to time already served and a period of illegal detention prior to the tribunal's creation, leaving Duch with a net sentence that means he could eventually be released.

Some Cambodians felt the punishment fell short given the scale of his crimes. 

"He killed thousands of people," said Bou Meng, another S-21 survivor who wept as the judgment was read. "My wife died in that place. How can a man who destroyed so many lives ever be allowed to walk free?"

### A nation's long road to justice

The verdict represents a major milestone for the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), a joint tribunal established by the Cambodian government and the United Nations after years of agonizing political negotiations. 

An estimated 1.7 to 2 million people—nearly a quarter of Cambodia's population at the time—died from starvation, forced labor, disease, and mass executions under the ultra-Maoist vision of Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, who died in the jungle in 1998 without ever facing trial.

While Duch is the first major figure to be convicted, prosecutors are preparing for subsequent trials involving higher-ranking political leaders of the regime, including Nuon Chea, known as "Brother Number Two," and Khieu Samphan, the regime's former head of state.

For many in Cambodia, where the scars of the genocide remain deeply visible, Duch's trial has served as a painful but necessary step toward national reconciliation.

"This is not just about one man," said trial prosecutor Chea Leang. "This is about telling the victims that their suffering was seen, that the truth was documented, and that those responsible for nightmare regimes will ultimately be held accountable."

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — The UN-backed tribunal in Phnom Penh resumed proceedings today in the landmark trial of Kaing Guek Eav, the former Khmer Rouge prison commander better known as "Duch." The trial marks a long-awaited legal reckoning for one of the 20th century’s darkest chapters, as the court delves into the systematic torture and murder committed under Duch’s command at the infamous S-21 Tuol Sleng prison.

Duch, 66, a former mathematics teacher turned chief bureaucrat of death for the ultra-Maoist regime, faces charges of crimes against humanity, war crimes, premeditated murder, and torture. He is the first senior figure of the Khmer Rouge leadership to stand trial before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), a joint tribunal established by the Cambodian government and the United Nations.

Inside the purpose-built courtroom on the outskirts of the capital, Duch sat quietly behind bulletproof glass, wearing a light-blue shirt and reading glasses. Observers noted his calm, composed demeanor—a stark contrast to the horrific evidence presented by prosecutors detailing his meticulous oversight of the regime’s premier interrogation center.

---

### The Machinery of Death: S-21 and the Killing Fields

Between April 1975 and January 1979, the Khmer Rouge, led by Marxist revolutionary Pol Pot, attempted to reset Cambodian society to "Year Zero." The regime emptied cities, abolished currency and religion, and forced the population into vast rural labor collectives. 

Historians estimate that between **1.7 and 2.2 million people**—nearly a quarter of Cambodia's total population at the time—perished under the regime due to mass executions, forced labor, starvation, and untreated disease.

At the center of this apparatus was Tuol Sleng, a former high school in Phnom Penh converted into the secret S-21 security prison. Under Duch’s leadership, S-21 functioned with chilling administrative efficiency. Suspected "traitors," intellects, civil servants, and even loyal cadres caught in the regime's paranoid purges were brought to the facility alongside their families.

According to court documentation, an estimated **15,000 to 18,000 men, women, and children** passed through the gates of S-21. Victims were subjected to waterboarding, beatings, electrocution, and medical experimentation to extract false confessions of espionage before being transported to the Choeung Ek killing fields outside the city to be executed.

Fewer than 12 people are known to have survived S-21.

---

### Voices of the Survivors

For the handful of living survivors and the hundreds of victims' family members attending the trial as Civil Parties, the resumption of the trial brings an overwhelming wave of painful memories alongside a desperate hope for closure.

Chum Mey, 79, one of the few men to walk out of S-21 alive because his skills as a mechanic were needed to repair prison machinery, delivered an emotional testimony during the proceedings.

> *"They tore out my fingernails, they shocked me with electricity until I lost consciousness, and they forced me to confess to being a CIA agent—a word I didn't even understand at the time,"* Mey told reporters outside the courtroom. *"I do not want revenge. I want justice, and I want Duch to tell the whole truth. I want to know why so many innocent people had to die."*

Another survivor, Bou Meng, an artist who was spared so he could paint propaganda portraits of Pol Pot, recalled the moment he was torn from his family upon arrival at the prison.

> *"I lost my wife at S-21. I never saw her again after we were processed,"* Meng said, holding a painted portrait of his late wife. *"Every day I think about her suffering. Duch has asked for forgiveness, but forgiveness cannot come without the full truth. He must explain his orders and name those who gave them."*

---

### The Strategy of the Prosecution and the Defense

International Co-Prosecutor Robert Petit argued before the judges that Duch was not merely a passive subordinate following orders, but an enthusiastic administrator who refined interrogation techniques and actively managed the extermination process.

"The evidence will demonstrate that the accused held complete authority over S-21," Petit stated. "He personally authorized torture, signed off on execution lists, and ensured that no one left the facility alive."

Duch has taken an unusual stance compared to other surviving Khmer Rouge leaders—such as Nuon Chea ("Brother Number Two") and Khieu Samphan—who have largely denied knowledge of the atrocities. Duch has admitted his role as the head of S-21, offered public apologies, and acknowledged that atrocities were committed under his watch.

However, his defense team, led by French attorney François Roux and Cambodian co-counsel Kar Savuth, contends that Duch was operating within a deadly chain of command where disobedience meant certain death for him and his family.

"I was a slave to the party," Duch stated during a previous hearing, reiterating his defense. "I acted out of fear for my life. If I had refused the orders of the higher committee, I would have been killed immediately, and someone else would have taken my place."

---

### A Test for Justice and National Healing

The trial is seen as a crucial test for Cambodia, a country still grappling with the deep physical and psychological scars left by the Khmer Rouge era three decades later. It is also a test for the hybrid court model, which has faced criticism over slow proceedings, high financial costs, and allegations of political interference from the current Cambodian government.

Despite these challenges, the atmosphere outside the court today was filled with quiet reverence. Buses organized by NGOs brought hundreds of monks, students, and elderly villagers from remote provinces to witness the trial live via video monitors.

For many, seeing Duch stand trial offers a long-overdue acknowledgment of their suffering.

"Thirty years is a long time to wait," said Norng Chan Phal, who was just eight years old when he was rescued from S-21 by invading Vietnamese troops in 1979 after his mother was executed. "My mother cannot come back, but seeing the man responsible for her death answer for his crimes means her memory is finally being honored."

The trial is expected to continue over the coming months, with dozens of expert witnesses, former prison guards, and survivors slated to take the stand. If convicted, Duch faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, as the ECCC does not have the authority to impose the death penalty.

Here is a news story written in the style of an international news agency report covering that historic moment in July 2010.

***

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — More than three decades after the fall of the ultra-communist Khmer Rouge regime, a UN-backed tribunal in Phnom Penh has delivered the first-ever war crimes conviction against one of its senior officials, marking a long-awaited moment of justice for the victims of the "Killing Fields."

Kaing Guek Eav, the 67-year-old former mathematics teacher better known as "Duch," was sentenced on Monday to 35 years in prison for crimes against humanity, war crimes, murder, and torture. The tribunal reduced his sentence to 19 years to account for time already served and a period of illegal detention prior to the trial.

Duch was the feared commander of the notorious Tuol Sleng prison—coded S-21—in Phnom Penh. Between 1975 and 1979, an estimated 15,000 to 18,000 men, women, and children were brought to the converted high school, where they were systematically tortured into confessing to fabricated acts of treason before being transported to the nearby Choeung Ek fields to be executed. Fewer than a dozen people are known to have survived S-21.

"The Chamber finds that Kaing Guek Eav was responsible for the deaths of at least 12,272 victims," declared the court's Cambodian president, Judge Nil Nonn, as he read the lengthy judgment before a packed courtroom. 

Duch stood silently, showing little emotion as the verdict was read. 

During the trial, which began in 2009, Duch admitted his role as the chief executioner of the regime's security apparatus and offered tears and public apologies to the victims. He detailed how meticulous records and photographs were kept of every prisoner who passed through his hands, driven by a fear of being purged himself by the regime's top leadership. 

An estimated 1.7 million to 2 million Cambodians—roughly a quarter of the country’s population—died from execution, starvation, forced labor, and medical neglect under the reign of Pol Pot, the regime's leader, who died in 1998 without ever facing trial.

Outside the court, hundreds of Cambodians gathered, while thousands more watched live television broadcasts in villages across the country. For many survivors, the trial was an essential step toward national healing, though the reduced sentence sparked mixed emotions.

"I cannot accept this sentence," said Chum Mey, 79, one of the few living survivors of S-21 who testified during the trial. "My wife and children were killed. To give him a sentence where he might one day walk free does not feel like justice."

Despite the mixed reactions to the length of the prison term, human rights advocates hailed the verdict as a historic milestone for international law and a crucial precedent for Cambodia’s fragile judicial system. 

"This is a monumentally historic day," said Rupert Skilbeck, a lawyer representing victims in the case. "For 30 years, the victims waited for an answer. Today, an independent court declared that Duch was guilty of terrible crimes, and the truth has been permanently recorded."

The court, officially known as the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), was established jointly by the United Nations and the Cambodian government in 2006. 

Duch's trial was seen as a test case for the tribunal. Attention now turns to the court’s second case, which involves the regime's surviving top political leaders, including "Brother Number Two" Nuon Chea and former head of state Khieu Samphan, both of whom face charges of genocide.

*(Note: Following an appeal by prosecutors in 2012, the supreme court chamber of the tribunal overturned the 35-year sentence and imposed a life sentence on Duch. He remained in prison until his death in September 2020.)*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed news article about Duch, the former math teacher who ran the Tuol Sleng torture prison under Pol Pot.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE ARCHITECT OF S-21: HOW A MATH TEACHER BECAME THE KHMER ROUGE’S CHIEF EXECUTIONER**

**By Lines / Foreign Desk**  
**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — To his former high school students in the Cambodian countryside, Kaing Guek Eav was known as a quiet, meticulous mathematics teacher who demanded absolute precision. To the world, he would become known by his revolutionary nom de guerre, "Duch"—the chief warden of Tuol Sleng, the most infamous torture center of Pol Pot’s brutal Khmer Rouge regime.

Between 1975 and 1979, Duch transformed a former Phnom Penh high school into a terrifyingly efficient death factory known as Security Prison 21 (S-21). Under his precise, bureaucratic command, an estimated 18,000 men, women, and children walked through the gates of S-21. Fewer than a dozen survived.

Duch, who died in September 2020 at the age of 77 while serving a life sentence for crimes against humanity, remains one of history’s most chilling examples of how ordinary intellect can be weaponized in the service of total totalitarian evil.

---

### From the Classroom to the Revolution

Born in 1942 in Kampong Thom province, Kaing Guek Eav was a star student who excelled in academics, particularly mathematics. In the mid-1960s, he earned his teaching credentials and taught at a local high school. Colleagues and former students remembered him as a disciplined, somewhat dry instructor who insisted on order and logical rigor.

However, as Cambodia plunged into political turmoil during the Vietnam War era, Duch grew increasingly radicalized. Drawn to communist ideology and infuriated by the corruption of the U.S.-backed Lon Nol government, he joined the underground Communist Party of Kampuchea—the Khmer Rouge—in 1967.

His aptitude for organization and unquestioning loyalty quickly brought him to the attention of the party's senior leadership. During the civil war, Duch was placed in charge of security camps in the jungle, where he honed the brutal interrogation and execution techniques he would later standardize in the capital.

When Pol Pot’s forces captured Phnom Penh on April 17, 1975, initiating "Year Zero" and declaring the creation of Democratic Kampuchea, Duch was tasked with a vital mission: protecting the revolution from internal enemies.

---

### S-21: The Factory of Confessions

Duch took over Tuol Svay Prey High School in central Phnom Penh, stripping the classrooms of their blackboards and replacing them with brick cells, iron shackles, and torture apparatuses. Renamed S-21, the facility was designed not for long-term detention, but as a processing center for suspected traitors before their execution.

Applying his mathematical precision to the machinery of terror, Duch created a hyper-bureaucratized system. Every prisoner brought to S-21 was photographed, interviewed, tortured until they confessed to absurd plots involving the CIA, the KGB, or Vietnamese intelligence, and then marked for "destruction."

Duch kept immaculate records. He personally annotated hundreds of prisoner confessions, often writing neat, cold instructions in the margins: *"Kill them all,"* *"Beat them until they tell the truth,"* or *"Keep for interrogation, then destroy."*

Prisoners were subjected to waterboarding, electric shocks, beatings, and medical experimentation. Once a confession was extracted, the prisoners were loaded onto trucks at night and driven to a nearby orchard in Choeung Ek—a site now known globally as the "Killing Fields"—where they were executed with iron bars, machetes, or agricultural tools to save bullets.

"I am responsible for all the crimes committed at S-21," Duch would later admit. "Including the deaths of thousands of innocent people."

---

### Twenty Years in the Shadows

When the Vietnamese army invaded Cambodia and ousted the Khmer Rouge in January 1979, Duch fled into the jungles near the Thai border. As the regime collapsed, he ordered the destruction of prison records, though thousands of detailed photographs and written confessions were left behind—forming the damning archive that would later convict him.

For two decades, Duch vanished. He changed his name to Hang Pin, moved his family between border villages, and worked as a teacher and aid worker. In the late 1990s, after his wife was killed in a mysterious attack, Duch converted to born-again Christianity, framing his spiritual shift as a path to redemption.

His past finally caught up with him in 1999, when British photojournalist Nic Dunlop tracked him down in western Cambodia. Duch did not deny his identity; instead, he spoke openly about his role at S-21, paving the way for his arrest by Cambodian authorities.

---

### The First to Face Justice

Duch’s trial before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC)—a hybrid United Nations-Cambodian tribunal—began in 2009. He was the first senior Khmer Rouge figure to be brought to trial (Case 001).

Unlike other regime leaders who denied all knowledge of atrocities, Duch offered a complex, unsettling defense. He acknowledged his role, admitted guilt, and expressed remorse to the victims and their families. He spent days on the witness stand detailing the inner workings of the regime's terror apparatus.

However, his defense also relied heavily on the argument that he was merely a low-level administrator following orders under threat of his own death. He presented himself as a victim of a system he could not escape.

"Anyone who was ordered to go to S-21 knew they were already dead if they refused," Duch testified.

Prosecutors counter-argued that Duch was not a reluctant follower, but an enthusiastic administrator who refined torture techniques and expressed pride in his efficiency. 

Survivors of S-21, such as painter Bou Meng and mechanic Chum Mey—two of the fewer than a dozen people who survived the prison because their skills were useful to the regime—confronted Duch in court. They recounted the physical and psychological devastation wrought under his command.

---

### Judgment and Legacy

In July 2010, the tribunal found Duch guilty of crimes against humanity, war crimes, murder, and torture, initially sentencing him to 35 years in prison. Following widespread outrage over the perceived leniency of the sentence, an appeals court extended his term to life imprisonment in 2012.

Duch spent his final years behind bars at Kandal Provincial Prison, his health deteriorating until his death from respiratory illness in 2020.

Today, Tuol Sleng stands as the Genocide Museum in Phnom Penh, preserved much as Duch left it in 1979. The rust-stained iron beds, the torture implements, and row upon row of black-and-white portraits of terrified men, women, and children stare back at thousands of visitors each year.

Historians and criminologists view Duch's transformation as a haunting study in human psychology—a chilling testament to how an ordinary, educated man, governed by strict discipline and ideological fervor, could become the administrator of horror.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a news report about the trial of former prison chief Duch, including mentions of S-21, quotes from Robert Petit and Youk Chhang, and a survivor's perspective.
counterfactuals.output:
**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — Thirty years after the fall of one of the 20th century's deadliest regimes, Kaing Guek Eav, the notorious former prison chief better known as "Duch," stood in the dock today as the UN-backed tribunal into the atrocities of the Khmer Rouge opened its landmark first trial.

Duch, 66, faces charges of crimes against humanity, war crimes, murder, and torture for his role as the commandant of Tuol Sleng—the high school turned interrogation center codenamed S-21. Between 1975 and 1979, an estimated 15,000 to 18,000 men, women, and children passed through the gates of S-21. Meticulously cataloged, photographed, and tortured into confessing to fabricated acts of treason, virtually all were subsequently sent to the nearby "killing fields" of Choeung Ek for execution. 

As the proceedings opened at the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), International Co-Prosecutor Robert Petit emphasized the profound weight the trial carries for a nation long denied legal recourse. 

"This trial represents the culmination of years of effort to hold accountable those who committed the most heinous crimes," Petit told the court. "For the people of Cambodia, it is a crucial step toward breaking the culture of impunity that has haunted this country for decades and establishing a historical record grounded in law."

Unlike other surviving senior leaders of the ultra-Maoist regime who have denied knowledge of the mass killings, Duch has publicly expressed remorse for his actions. However, his defense strategy is expected to argue that he was merely a subordinate following strict orders under threat of his own execution. 

For historians and researchers, the trial serves as a vital reckoning with the country’s dark past. Youk Chhang, director of the Documentation Center of Cambodia (DC-Cam), which spent years gathering millions of pages of archives, photographs, and testimonies to support the prosecution, noted that the trial extends far beyond the fate of a single defendant.

"Duch was the meticulous bureaucrat of genocide, the man who oversaw the administrative machinery of death at S-21," Chhang said outside the courtroom. "This trial is not just about one man’s guilt; it is about revealing the truth and restoring dignity to the victims. It is about writing an undeniable history so that future generations of Cambodians can finally move forward."

Inside the gallery, seated among hundreds of citizens, Buddhist monks, and international observers, were the handful of individuals who managed to leave S-21 alive. Fewer than a dozen people are believed to have survived the prison.

Bou Meng, a 68-year-old artist who survived S-21 only because he was tasked with painting portraits of Khmer Rouge supreme leader Pol Pot, wiped away tears as he watched his former captor behind a bulletproof glass barrier. Meng’s wife, Ma Yoeun, was dragged away by guards during their detention and never seen again.

"I have waited thirty years for this day," Bou Meng said, his voice shaking with emotion. "Every night, I still hear the screams of the tortured and see the face of my wife. I want Duch to look me in the eye and tell me why she had to die. I do not want revenge, but I need justice before I close my eyes forever."

The trial of Duch is widely seen as a litmus test for the hybrid court, which combines Cambodian and international law. As the tribunal prepares to hear weeks of harrowing testimony, the people of Cambodia watch closely, hoping that the long-delayed legal process will finally bring a measure of closure to a tragedy that cost an estimated 1.7 million lives.
